title: Constant force amplifies pulse solitons via polarization coupling in mechanical metamaterials
abstract: Unlike kink solitons with nonzero topological charge, pulse solitons cannot be driven by the experimentally most easily implemented constant force because of their zero topological charge. Here, we focus on a vector soliton with two polarization components: a pulse soliton component (rotation) and a kink soliton component (translation). We apply a constant force at the mass centers of the units, thereby driving the translational component with a constant force. Numerical simulations show that energy injected into the translational component can be transferred simultaneously to the rotational component through coupling, thereby achieving equal amplification of positive and negative pulses. Next, we change the application of this constant force to eccentric loading and find that the initially symmetric amplification of positive and negative solitons gradually becomes asymmetric over time. These phenomena are all explained by a theoretical model based on the adiabatic approximation, which gives a quantitative relation for the amplitude evolution, while the higher-order correction terms arising from the coupling effect also explain the origin of asymmetric transmission under eccentric driving. Our results demonstrate that vector solitons possess a unique capability for pulse soliton amplification by a constant force through polarization coupling and that this coupling can further modulate the symmetry between positive and negative pulses.
summary: This paper analyzes the amplification of pulse solitons in mechanical metamaterials driven by a constant external force. It demonstrates that polarization coupling allows the force to drive the soliton, and critically, that shifting the force application point breaks the symmetry, leading to unequal amplification of positive versus negative pulses. The work provides a theoretical framework for understanding symmetry breaking in nonlinear wave dynamics.
main_problem: The study investigates how a constant external force amplifies pulse solitons in mechanical metamaterials via polarization coupling, and how this coupling can break the symmetry of this amplification.
main_result: Vector solitons can be amplified by a constant force through polarization coupling, and applying the force eccentrically breaks the symmetry, leading to unequal amplification of positive and negative pulses.
method: The analysis employs numerical simulations, continuum limit approximations, and the adiabatic approximation to derive energy balance equations and amplitude evolution equations.
model_or_system: The system is a mechanical metamaterial modeled as a chain of coupled units with two polarization components: translational ($U_i$) and rotational ($	heta_i$). The dynamics are governed by coupled equations of motion incorporating coupling springs.
key_observables: Soliton amplitude evolution ($A(T)$), energy balance ($dE/dT$), and the symmetry/asymmetry of amplification between positive and negative pulses.
important_parameters: The constant driving force ($F$), the eccentricity parameter ($b$), and the coupling constants ($K_	heta, K_s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on the adiabatic approximation, assuming the soliton retains its form while being driven by a weak external force ($F \ll 1$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic model, the perfect symmetry of amplification under central force application, and the resulting asymmetric amplification when the force is applied eccentrically.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the coupled discrete equations of motion, deriving the continuum limit and energy balance, applying the adiabatic approximation, and finally analyzing the symmetry-preserving and symmetry-breaking effects of the external force.
why_interesting: The study models energy transfer and nonlinear wave dynamics in a mechanical system, which shares mathematical parallels with driven nonlinear oscillators and coupled field theories relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems.
